summary: This informational document defines a reference framework for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance in TRILL networks. It focuses on fault and performance management.

eli5.summary: Networks need tools to check whether they are broken or slow. This sets the plan for what checks TRILL networks should have.

questions: how do you monitor trill networks
how do you find faults in trill
subtitle: A framework for monitoring the health and performance of TRILL networks.

tldr.problem: TRILL networks need ways to detect faults and measure performance to ensure reliable communication. Existing OAM approaches do not fit TRILL's unique characteristics, such as support for arbitrary link technologies and non-congruent paths.
tldr.mechanism: This framework defines maintenance domains, endpoints and intermediate points, and specifies both proactive (continuous monitoring) and on-demand (manual diagnostics) mechanisms for detecting connectivity problems and measuring packet loss and delay.
tldr.outcome: Operators can now monitor TRILL networks systematically using standard OAM concepts adapted for TRILL's layer model and path independence. The framework serves as the basis for future TRILL OAM protocol specifications.

today: RFC 7174 is an Informational RFC that remains active and has not been obsoleted. It establishes the foundational framework for TRILL OAM that subsequent RFCs build upon for specific protocol implementations.

sections.title: TRILL and Network Health Checks
sections.content:
TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links) is a routing protocol that lets Ethernet work over large, complex networks with multiple paths between devices. Unlike traditional Ethernet bridges, TRILL can work over any link technology and does not require the same path for traffic going back and forth.

OAM (Operations, Administration, and Maintenance) refers to the tools and procedures that keep networks running smoothly. This framework focuses on two critical aspects: finding problems (Fault Management) and measuring how well the network performs (Performance Monitoring). Operators can use these capabilities to detect failures before users notice them and to monitor network quality in real time.
sections.eli5: TRILL is a way to make networks more flexible and efficient. OAM is about checking on the network's health, like a doctor checking a patient.

sections.title: OAM Structure in TRILL
sections.content:
TRILL OAM sits as a distinct layer between the port's encapsulation function and the forwarding engine on each router, called an RBridge. This layer works alongside other OAM mechanisms: CFM (Connectivity Fault Management) runs at the application and transport layers, BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) handles fast link failure detection, and link-specific OAM handles physical link management.

The framework defines three levels of monitoring granularity. Network OAM tests connectivity across the entire TRILL network using a test VLAN or label. Service OAM monitors actual customer VLANs. Flow OAM provides the finest granularity by monitoring individual data flows, though this poses scalability challenges.

OAM functions are organized into Maintenance Domains, which are administrative boundaries managed by a single operator. Within a domain, a Maintenance Entity links two points for monitoring. The endpoints (MEPs) are active and send heartbeat messages; intermediate points (MIPs) passively forward messages and respond to specific queries.
sections.eli5: The network is divided into zones, each with watching stations. Some stations actively send health checks; others just listen and report back when asked. This keeps the network organized and lets different parts be managed separately.

sections.title: Finding and Diagnosing Failures
sections.content:
Fault management has two modes. Proactive monitoring runs continuously without operator intervention. MEPs periodically exchange Continuity Check messages to verify reachability between service endpoints. These checks detect four types of problems: loss of connectivity to remote MEPs, unexpected connections between isolated networks (mismerge), unexpectedly reaching a MEP you should not reach, and timing mismatches in heartbeat periods.

On-demand fault management is triggered manually when an operator suspects a problem. Connectivity Verification tests whether a specific path is working, supporting both unicast and multicast with various granularities (the entire network, a specific VLAN, or individual flows). Fault Isolation traces the path hop-by-hop to pinpoint where the break is. Because TRILL allows asymmetric paths (different routes going forward and backward), operators must run diagnostics in both directions to fully isolate faults.

When faults are detected, the framework supports two types of defect signals. Forward Defect Indication alerts the network to problems detected by lower-layer mechanisms and propagates away from the failure. Reverse Defect Indication (RDI) signals loss of connectivity back towards the source, enabling single-sided monitoring where one MEP can detect if the other side is broken.
sections.eli5: The network watches for broken connections in two ways: constantly checking if everything is still connected, or running specific diagnostic tests when something seems wrong. When a break is found, the network sends alert messages so operators and other parts of the network know about it.

sections.title: Measuring Network Performance
sections.content:
Performance monitoring is optional but important for understanding network quality. Packet Loss measurement sends synthetic OAM packets counted only by the ports that should receive them. This provides a statistical view of data loss, since TRILL's multipoint-to-multipoint nature means user data packets can be delivered more widely than intended due to broadcasting and flooding. One-way loss monitoring allows a source RBridge to send probes while the target calculates loss. Two-way monitoring lets the source measure loss in both directions by sending probes and receiving replies.

Packet Delay measurement uses timestamps at fixed offsets in OAM packets to enable hardware-based timing. One-way measurement requires the two RBridges to have synchronized clocks; two-way measurement can calculate round-trip delay without clock sync. The framework recommends hardware implementations record timestamps as close to the physical wire as practical for maximum accuracy.
sections.eli5: The network measures two important things: whether packets are getting lost and how long it takes for them to get from one place to another. Special test packets help measure these without interfering with real traffic.

sections.title: Configuring and Operating TRILL OAM
sections.content:
To keep TRILL simple, OAM configuration should use defaults and auto-discovery where possible. Operators configure maintenance domains with a domain name and level (for hierarchical nesting), maintenance associations for specific VLAN or label contexts, and maintenance endpoints with identifiers, direction (UP or DOWN), and associated interfaces. The framework recommends expanding the MEP identifier range from 1 to 8191 to 1 to 65535 so the RBridge nickname can serve as a default value.

Different operations require different parameters. Continuity Check settings include transmission interval, loss threshold (how many missed heartbeats trigger an alarm; 3 is recommended), the VLAN or label to use, and hop count limits. Connectivity Verification parameters specify the target RBridge, VLAN, flow information, timeout (5 seconds recommended), repeat count, and reply mode (in-band or out-of-band). Similar parameter sets apply to Fault Isolation and the optional performance measurements.

The framework also specifies how the network should identify OAM messages. Since OAM packets must mimic data packets to accurately test the path, an Alert flag in the TRILL header signals control traffic. Combined with an OAM Ethertype (a 2-byte code), this reliably identifies OAM frames without disrupting normal forwarding and ECMP load balancing.
sections.eli5: Networks need clear rules for how many checks to run, how long to wait for replies, and which paths to check. The framework sets up these rules as defaults so operators do not have to configure every detail.
